### Contributing guidelines

- [x] I have read [CONTRIBUTING.md](https://github.com/echasnovski/mini.nvim/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md)
- [x] I have read [CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md](https://github.com/echasnovski/mini.nvim/blob/main/CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md)
- [x] I have updated 'mini.nvim' to latest version of the `main` branch

### Module(s)

mini.files

### Neovim version

0.11.x

### Description

Note that I haven't personally reproduced this bug myself, it seems to only occur on Windows. I was made aware of it while helping a friend who was trying out Neovim for the first time; we confirmed it together during a screen sharing session. So I'm mainly reporting this second-hand, just to raise awareness in case others hit the same issue.

## The issue

On Windows, after opening a file via mini.files, pressing q to exit the explorer causes Neovim to hang for a few seconds (roughly 5-6s), then eventually resumes/cleans up as expected. There's no crash or error, just a noticeable and unexplained delay before closing the mini.files window.

The configuration in use is extremely simple, just calling mini.files.open() with the current buffer or cwd:

```lua
---@module "mini.files"

---@type LazyPluginSpec
local Spec = {
  "mini.files", virtual = true, event = "VeryLazy",

  keys = {
    {
      "<leader>f",
      function()
        require("mini.files").open(vim.api.nvim_buf_get_name(0))
      end,
      desc = "Open mini.files (directory of current file)",
    },
    {
      "<leader>F",
      function()
        require("mini.files").open()
      end,
      desc = "Open mini.files (cwd)",
    },
  },

  -- opts shouldn't call setup, as this module self-export through _G.
  config = function (_, opts)
    require ("mini.files").setup (opts)
  end,
}

return Spec
```

While nothing unusual seems to be going on, just for completeness here's the actual config used during the during said session and as you may see, it's a fairly minimal setup, mostly basic LSP utilities, nothing exotic or experimental that would obviously interfere with mini.files:

[nvim.zip](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/21390992/nvim.zip)


### Reproduction

Unfortunately, I can't provide a clean nvim-repro setup for this. Walking them through setting up a separate NVIM_APPNAME environment and going through repro steps felt like a bit too much to ask while they're still just getting their bearings with Neovim in general. Didn't want to turn a fun first experience into a bug hunt.

For completeness:

Found with Neovim 0.11.3 and Windows Terminal on Windows 11.

comment_data.body:
Thanks for the issue!

I can not reproduce: neither in my personal config nor with the provided zipped one (why does it have inlined 'lazy.nvim', 'mini.test', and 'mini.doc'?). I am afraid without actually reliable minimal way to reproduce I can not help much (I don't have access to the Windows machine and testing on CI requires a "mini.files only" way to reproduce the issue).

I am also at least 95% sure that this has nothing to do with 'mini.files' and at least 50% sure that this has nothing *directly* to do with OS. This looks like either a result of a misconfiguration or a coincidence. Judging by the description, my ideas would be:
- The "... after opening a file via mini.files, pressing q to exit the explorer ..." part implies that this can be reproduced *only* after opening a file. In that case there might be an active LSP/tree-sitter being involved, which somehow slow down and/or block the whole Neovim instance.

    Ways to test it would be to:
    - Press `q` just after opening explorer and not after opening a file. If fast - the issue is probably in the opened file.
    - Try to open file that is not LSP/tree-sitter related, i.e. just a regular empty 'file'. If fast - the issue is probably related to other plugins and/or LSP/tree-sitter.

- I looked into config and didn't find anything, but my first thought was that there is some buffer-local mapping that starts from `q` that is created in 'mini.files' buffers. That way pressing `q` would make Neovim wait for the possible next key until its timeout (usually 1 second though and not 4-5).

    Ways to test it would be to:
    - Set up `config.mappings.close` in `require('mini.files').setup()` to be something else than `'q'`. For example, `P`.
    - Execute `:nmap q` when inside an active explorer and see the output. It should show only a single `q` mapping that comes directly from 'mini.files'.

A more strong evidence that this shouldn't come from 'mini.files' is that pressing `q` to close explorer [is tested](https://github.com/echasnovski/mini.nvim/blob/432a0614f8dc38715892b0eec537716457ea4c2f/tests/test_files.lua#L2868-L2869) on all platforms (Windows included). Just to be double sure, I also tested that it actually hides floating windows and [it also does that](https://github.com/echasnovski/mini.nvim/actions/runs/16477098586/job/46581554438).

---

All in all, I am going to close this as most probably not an issue with 'mini.files'. If you have new data, I'll try to help more or reopen if enough evidence.

OK, I was able to reproduce the issue on my system after upgrading. The root cause appears to be related to Tree-sitter. However, what's odd is that Neovim itself doesn't hang in the traditional sense, it's still running, but it stops responding to input entirely. No keystrokes are processed

So technically it's not a freeze or crash, but something is blocking or breaking input handling altogether, which makes it feel like a hang.

I still need to dig deeper and try to isolate exactly what's triggering it. Will follow up once/if I've narrowed it down further.

The `nvim-treesitter` docs say that calling `require('nvim-treesitter').install(filetype)` should be a no-op if the parser is already installed. That's the expectation, at least. But in practice, that doesn't seem to hold.

Here's the setup we're using:

```lua
config = function (_, opts)
    vim.iter(opts.ensure_installed):each(function (ft)
        vim.api.nvim_create_autocmd("FileType", {
            pattern = { ft },
            callback = function ()
                require("nvim-treesitter").install(ft) -- expected to be a no-op if already installed
...
```

The idea is simple: if the parser for a given filetype isn't there yet, install it when we first open a matching file. Once installed, it shouldn't need to do anything else. But what actually happens is that every time we launch Neovim and open a file, even one we just edited a few minutes ago, it goes ahead and recompiles the parser from scratch like nothing was cached.

That's already a bit surprising, and expensive. But the real issue is that while this compile step looks like it's happening in the background, it isn't. Input is completely frozen until the compilation finishes. This goes against what the documentation promises: that installs should be asynchronous and non-blocking.

It took me a while to realize what was going on, mostly because I hadn't updated my plugins in a bit. But once I did, the problem was immediately obvious. It feels like something changed upstream, possibly a regression, because this used to just quietly work not that long ago.

In any case, this isn't an issue with mini.files. It only appears that way at first because we typically use mini.files to open files, which is what ends up triggering the FileType event. So while mini.files might seem involved, it's just the entry point, any other method of opening files would produce the same behavior.

EDIT: **OK this only happen if treesitter-cli is not installed, relevant issue: https://github.com/nvim-treesitter/nvim-treesitter/issues/8010**

Thanks for the follow up!

> Here's the setup we're using:

A drive by suggestion: I'd create a single `FileType` autocommand with multiple filetypes as `pattern` instead of many autocommands. Not sure if it *really* is better performance, but it feels like it should be.

Or even a better approach would be something like checking which languages are not installed (here [one way to do it](https://github.com/echasnovski/nvim/blob/7fddcee453af02406bc6ce63743f3e8e46742f22/plugin/21_plugins.lua#L23-L24)) and create separate autocommands for each one with `once = true`. The `vim.treesitter.start()` can be a separate single autocommand with array `pattern`.

And beware that 'filetype' value might be different from tree-sitter parser/language name. Like `markdown-inline` is not a filetype. You can [use `vim.treesitter.language.get_filetypes()`](https://github.com/echasnovski/nvim/blob/7fddcee453af02406bc6ce63743f3e8e46742f22/plugin/21_plugins.lua#L28C52-L28C89) to get relevant filetypes.
